Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Gen. Ray Odierno, the top U.S. military commander in Iraq, said Sunday he believes U.S. troops will be out of the country by the end of 2011. Gen. Ray Odierno says the U.S. is working with Iraq to maintain security improvements as it looks to withdraw. On CNN's "State of the Union," chief national correspondent John King asked Odierno to rate his confidence, on a scale of 1 to 10, that U.S. troops would be out by the end of the timeline agreed by the U.S. and Iraqi governments. "As you ask me today, I believe it's a 10 -- that we will be gone by 2011," Odierno responded. One of the key architects of the troop "surge" strategy in Iraq, Odierno said conditions in the war-torn country have "improved significantly" in the past year or so. "Obviously, we still have some very serious incidents ... but, again, it's much safer," he said. Nine U.S. troops were killed in March, the lowest monthly toll since the beginning of the Iraq War in 2003, he said.  Watch Odierno share his assessment with CNN's John King » . "So, there's been a clear improvement of security here," Odierno said. "The issue is: Can we maintain that? Can the Iraqis maintain it? And that's what we're working through now. We want them to be able to maintain this stability as we pull out." But less than two weeks into April, the U.S. toll for the month is already at nine. Asked whether the attacks were a sign of increased coordinated violence, Odierno responded that "there are some cells out there who are still capable of conducting suicide attacks," though he described the cells as "very small."  Watch as general discusses joining Facebook » . The U.S. military has made it more difficult for foreign fighters to get into Iraq through Syria, but there is still support for the Iraqi insurgency coming from Iran, he said. Mowaffak al-Rubaie, Iraqi national security adviser, said the Iraqi government is making improvements in handling its own security. "We, the government of Iraq and the security forces in Iraq are much more suited now for this fight," al-Rubaie told "State of the Union." "And we believe that now we are leading and we are planning and carrying out most of the combat operations in the country, " he said, "and the United States forces are moving or transitioning to a more support role, more training, more providing more logistical support, rather than engaging in a huge military or kinetic combat operations." Al-Rubaie was mum when asked how President Obama has differed from former President George W. Bush.  Watch al-Rubaie discuss Iraq's future » . "I don't want to elaborate on differences," al-Rubaie said. "But I believe that President Obama understands the situation in Iraq and I believe he wants to stick by ... the withdrawal agreement." Odierno described Obama as "very attentive." "He listens. He's incredibly intelligent. He talks through the issues," Odierno said. "He makes a decision and then we execute those decisions, and that's all you can expect out of your commander-in-chief. And I've been very pleased with the interaction that I've been able to have with him."

On CNN’s “State of the Union,” chief national correspondent John King asked Odierno to rate, on a scale of 1 to 10, his confidence that U.S. troops would leave by the deadline agreed upon by the U.S. and Iraqi governments.

“As you ask me today, I believe it’s a 10 — that we will be gone by 2011,” Odierno responded.

One of the key architects of the troop “surge” strategy in Iraq, Odierno said conditions in the war-torn country have “improved significantly” over the past year or so.

However, less than two weeks into April, the U.S. death toll for the month had already reached nine.

Asked whether the attacks signaled an increase in coordinated violence, Odierno said that “there are some cells out there who are still capable of conducting suicide attacks,” though he described those cells as “very small.”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Gen. Ray Odierno, the senior U.S. military commander in Iraq, said Sunday that he was fully confident American forces would leave Iraq by the end of 2011.

Speaking with CNN chief national correspondent John King on “State of the Union,” Odierno said the United States was cooperating with Iraq to preserve recent security gains while preparing for withdrawal.

King asked Odierno to assess, from 1 to 10, how certain he was that U.S. forces would depart by the deadline established by the American and Iraqi governments. Odierno rated his confidence a 10, saying he believed U.S. troops would be gone by 2011.

Odierno, who helped design the Iraq troop “surge,” said the country’s conditions had become substantially better over roughly the previous year. Although serious attacks continued to occur, he said Iraq was considerably safer.

According to Odierno, nine American service members died in March—the smallest monthly U.S. death toll since the Iraq War began in 2003. In a video, he discussed that assessment with King.

Odierno said the improvement in security was unmistakable, but the central question was whether it could be sustained, particularly by Iraqi forces. He said U.S. officials were working to ensure Iraq could preserve stability as American troops withdrew.

However, fewer than two weeks into April, nine U.S. troops had already been killed that month. When asked if the attacks indicated a rise in coordinated violence, Odierno said a limited number of remaining cells could still carry out suicide bombings, though he characterized those groups as very small. In another video segment, the general discussed joining Facebook.

Odierno also said the U.S. military had made it harder for foreign combatants to enter Iraq from Syria. Nevertheless, he said Iran continued to provide support to the Iraqi insurgency.

Iraqi national security adviser Mowaffak al-Rubaie said his government was becoming increasingly capable of managing the country’s security. Appearing on “State of the Union,” he said Iraq’s government and security forces were now better prepared for the conflict.

Al-Rubaie said Iraqi forces were directing, planning, and conducting most combat missions nationwide. Meanwhile, U.S. troops were shifting toward a supporting function focused more on training and logistics than on large-scale military—or “kinetic”—combat operations.

Asked to explain how President Obama differed from former President George W. Bush, al-Rubaie declined to provide details. In a separate video, he addressed Iraq’s future.

Al-Rubaie said he did not wish to expand on the differences between the two presidents. He added, however, that Obama understood circumstances in Iraq and appeared committed to honoring the withdrawal agreement.

Odierno called Obama highly attentive, exceptionally intelligent, and willing to listen and carefully discuss issues. He said the president made decisions that military commanders then carried out, which was all that could be expected from a commander in chief. Odierno added that he was very satisfied with his interactions with Obama.

Odierno noted that security conditions in Iraq had improved significantly. March saw the lowest monthly U.S. military death toll since the war began in 2003, reflecting a broader decline in violence. Gen. Ray Odierno offered an optimistic but measured assessment of security in Iraq as the United States prepared to end its military presence. He pointed to sharply lower casualty levels, a substantial decline in sectarian violence, and a dramatic reduction in the number of foreign fighters entering the country as evidence that conditions had improved. Although bombings, assassinations, and other attacks continued, he said they were generally being carried out by smaller insurgent cells that no longer had the capacity to threaten the Iraqi government or return the country to the widespread violence of earlier years.

Odierno emphasized that U.S. commanders were concentrating on preparing Iraqi security forces to assume full responsibility for the country. American troops were training and advising Iraqi soldiers and police, improving their ability to gather intelligence, coordinate operations, protect the population, and respond to terrorist attacks. Some weaknesses remained, particularly in logistics, intelligence, air defense, and the ability to sustain complex operations without American assistance. Nevertheless, Odierno believed Iraqi forces were increasingly capable of maintaining internal stability after the withdrawal.

He also noted that the flow of foreign militants into Iraq had fallen significantly from its peak. Better border controls, intelligence cooperation, and sustained pressure on extremist networks had made it more difficult for outside fighters to enter the country and join insurgent organizations. At the same time, he warned that Iranian support for armed groups remained a concern. Iran continued to provide certain militias with weapons, training, or financial assistance, contributing to attacks against U.S. and Iraqi personnel.

Despite these continuing threats, Odierno expressed complete confidence that all U.S. troops would leave Iraq by the end of 2011, in accordance with the security agreement between Washington and Baghdad. He said the withdrawal timetable was realistic because the overall security environment had improved so substantially and because Iraqi institutions had become stronger. The remaining violence, while serious, did not represent a return to full-scale insurgency or civil war.

Odierno’s assessment was therefore cautiously positive. Iraq had not eliminated terrorism, political tension, or foreign interference, and isolated groups remained capable of deadly attacks. Even so, he argued that the major security gains achieved in previous years had created the conditions for an orderly American departure and for Iraqi forces to take responsibility for preserving the country’s stability.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Gen. Ray Odierno saying he is fully confident U.S. troops will leave Iraq by the end of 2011.
counterfactuals.output:
# Odierno ‘fully confident’ U.S. troops will leave Iraq by end of 2011

**WASHINGTON —** Gen. Ray Odierno, the top U.S. commander in Iraq, said he is “fully confident” American troops will leave the country by the end of 2011, as required under an agreement between Washington and Baghdad.

Odierno said Iraqi security forces have continued to improve and are increasingly capable of taking responsibility for the country’s security, despite ongoing political uncertainty and sporadic insurgent attacks.

The withdrawal deadline was established in a 2008 security agreement between the United States and Iraq. Under the plan, U.S. combat operations were to end in 2010, with the remaining American forces departing by December 31, 2011.

Odierno acknowledged that militants still posed a threat, but said they lacked the strength to return Iraq to the widespread sectarian violence seen earlier in the war. U.S. forces would continue training and advising Iraqi troops as the drawdown proceeded, he said.

Any change to the timeline would require the Iraqi government to formally request a continued U.S. presence and Washington to approve it. Odierno indicated he did not expect that to happen.

The general’s comments came as Iraqi leaders worked to resolve political divisions following national elections. U.S. officials have warned that a prolonged dispute over forming a government could create openings for extremist groups, though they have maintained that the withdrawal remains on schedule.

The United States invaded Iraq in March 2003. At the height of the conflict, more than 160,000 American troops were deployed there.

counterfactuals.output:
## Report: Gen. Ray Odierno on CNN’s *State of the Union*

Gen. Ray Odierno, the senior U.S. commander in Iraq, presented a cautiously optimistic picture of the country. He said security had improved substantially, with violence well below its peak and Iraqi security forces increasingly taking responsibility. At the same time, he warned that the gains remained fragile. Al-Qaeda in Iraq and other militant groups could still carry out major attacks, while sectarian divisions, political instability, and Arab-Kurdish tensions remained potential threats.

### Withdrawal timeline

Odierno said the U.S. withdrawal was on schedule. The plan called for:

- U.S. combat forces to leave by the end of August 2010;
- roughly 50,000 troops to remain temporarily in advisory, training, and support roles; and
- all U.S. forces to leave by the end of 2011 under the U.S.-Iraq security agreement.

He stressed that commanders continually assessed conditions on the ground, but he did not argue for abandoning the timetable. Any U.S. presence beyond 2011, he indicated, would require a request from the Iraqi government and a new agreement.

### Assessment of President Obama

Odierno spoke positively of President Barack Obama as commander in chief. He described Obama as engaged, thoughtful, and willing to listen to military advice and ask detailed questions before making decisions. Although Odierno emphasized that his role was to provide professional military recommendations rather than political judgments, he conveyed confidence in Obama’s handling of Iraq and said the administration had carefully considered commanders’ views.

### Overall message

Odierno’s central point was that Iraq had made enough progress for the planned drawdown to proceed, but not enough for the United States or Iraqi leaders to become complacent. Security had improved markedly, yet the country’s long-term stability still depended on effective Iraqi governance, political reconciliation, and the continued development of its security forces.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed CNN.com article using quotes from Gen. Ray Odierno and Iraqi national security adviser Mowaffak al-Rubaie about security improvements, the changing U.S. military role, and the 2011 withdrawal agreement.
counterfactuals.output:
**Draft CNN.com-style article — quotations should be checked against original transcripts before publication**

# Improved security shifts U.S. mission in Iraq as 2011 deadline approaches

**By CNN Staff**  
**BAGHDAD, Iraq**

Years after sectarian violence pushed Iraq toward civil war, improved security is allowing the United States to reduce its combat role and place greater responsibility in the hands of Iraqi forces. But American and Iraqi officials caution that the gains remain fragile as both countries move toward a binding deadline for the withdrawal of all U.S. troops.

Gen. Ray Odierno, the top U.S. commander in Iraq, has said the decline in violence has enabled American troops to move away from leading daily operations and toward advising, training and supporting Iraqi security forces.

“Our mission has changed,” Odierno said in describing the transition. The emphasis, he said, is increasingly on helping Iraqi forces plan and conduct operations rather than having U.S. units take the lead.

The change follows a dramatic reduction in violence from the height of the conflict in 2006 and 2007. U.S. and Iraqi officials credit several factors: the American troop buildup commonly known as the “surge,” the growth of Iraqi army and police units, the decision by many Sunni tribal leaders to turn against al Qaeda in Iraq, and cease-fires observed by major Shiite militias.

Still, bombings and targeted attacks continue to expose weaknesses in Iraq’s security system. Insurgent groups retain the ability to strike crowded markets, religious sites and government buildings, often seeking to provoke renewed sectarian conflict.

Odierno has repeatedly warned that improved statistics do not mean Iraq is free of danger. He has said the period surrounding national elections, the formation of a new government and the continued drawdown of American forces will be critical to determining whether the security gains last.

## Iraqis take the lead

The changing U.S. role became more visible after American combat forces withdrew from Iraqi cities and towns under the terms of the security agreement between Washington and Baghdad. U.S. troops continued to provide intelligence, air support, logistics and specialized assistance, but Iraqi units assumed formal responsibility for urban security.

For Iraq’s government, that transfer was both a practical test and a symbol of restored sovereignty.

Mowaffak al-Rubaie, Iraq’s former national security adviser and a prominent supporter of the withdrawal timetable, described the transition bluntly: “The Americans are leaving. We are taking over.”

Al-Rubaie argued that Iraqi forces would not develop full independence if U.S. troops remained indefinitely. He also insisted that the withdrawal schedule was not merely an aspiration but a commitment negotiated and approved by both governments.

“There will be no American bases in Iraq after 2011,” al-Rubaie said, underscoring Baghdad’s position that the agreement does not provide for a permanent U.S. military presence.

The accord, formally known as the U.S.-Iraq Security Agreement, was signed in 2008. It required American combat forces to leave Iraqi cities by June 30, 2009, and called for all U.S. forces to withdraw from Iraq by December 31, 2011.

Unlike earlier plans based largely on conditions on the ground, the agreement established specific legal deadlines. Any extension would require new negotiations and the approval of Iraq’s government.

## A smaller but still significant U.S. presence

Even as American units pull back from front-line operations, the U.S. military continues to play an important supporting role.

Advisory teams work alongside Iraqi army and police units. American personnel assist with intelligence gathering, surveillance, bomb disposal, aviation and logistics — areas in which Iraqi forces have made progress but still face limitations.

The transition also requires commanders to balance two competing risks. A rapid reduction could leave Iraqi forces unable to confront insurgent networks or contain renewed political violence. But a prolonged American combat presence could undermine Iraqi sovereignty, fuel nationalist opposition and delay the development of self-sufficient security institutions.

Odierno has maintained that the withdrawal can proceed if security conditions continue to improve and Iraqi leaders resolve their disputes through politics rather than violence. His comments have reflected cautious confidence rather than a declaration of victory.

U.S. officials say Iraqi forces are increasingly capable of handling routine security operations. Questions remain, however, about their ability to protect the country’s borders, conduct complex intelligence operations, sustain equipment and respond to a major national crisis without substantial American assistance.

## Political disputes remain a threat

Iraq’s long-term stability depends on more than the strength of its army and police.

Disagreements over oil revenue, disputed territories and the powers of the central and regional governments remain unresolved. Tensions are particularly sharp in northern Iraq, where Kurdish and Arab leaders contest control of Kirkuk and other areas.

The integration of former Sunni fighters into the security forces and government employment is another source of concern. Many of those fighters joined U.S.-backed Awakening councils and helped drive al Qaeda-linked militants from their communities. Delays in providing them with jobs or salaries have raised fears that some could again become vulnerable to insurgent recruitment.

Sectarian mistrust also persists. Although large-scale fighting between Sunni and Shiite communities has sharply declined, spectacular attacks could still inflame old divisions.

Al-Rubaie and other Iraqi officials have argued that the country’s political leadership must match security progress with compromise and institution-building. Sovereignty, they say, involves not only the departure of foreign troops but also the ability of Iraq’s government to protect its citizens and settle disputes under the constitution.

## The meaning of 2011

For the United States, the 2011 deadline marks the end of a military presence that began with the March 2003 invasion and grew to more than 160,000 troops at the height of the surge.

For Iraq, the deadline represents a test of whether institutions built during years of war can function without a large foreign force.

The agreement does not guarantee that violence will end when the last American troops leave. Nor does it end the broader relationship between Washington and Baghdad. The two governments are expected to continue cooperation in diplomacy, trade, education and security, including possible military training conducted under separate arrangements.

But Iraqi officials have emphasized that any future relationship must respect the withdrawal accord and Iraqi sovereignty.

As the deadline approaches, the central question is no longer whether American forces will continue leading the war. It is whether Iraq’s government and security forces can preserve the gains made during the U.S. drawdown.

Odierno’s changing mission and al-Rubaie’s insistence on a complete withdrawal capture the two sides of that transition: American troops stepping back and Iraqi institutions stepping forward.

The decline in violence has created that opportunity. The durability of Iraq’s political system will determine whether it lasts.
